title: BCCI Pays ₹3,000 Crore in Annual Tax, Saikia Discloses at AGM
excerpt: BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia disclosed the board's income-tax outgo at the 95th Annual General Meeting, pushing back on perceptions of tax exemption as the Supreme Court seeks clarity on its status under the National Sports Governance Act.
body:
• BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia revealed at the board's 95th Annual General Meeting that the cricket body pays roughly ₹3,000 crore in income tax to the central government every year.
  • Saikia said the figure rebuts the long-running perception that the BCCI enjoys tax exemption, noting the board takes no government funding of any kind.
  • The Supreme Court recently asked the BCCI to clarify its tax position under the National Sports Governance Act; the board will file its response on October 27.
  • The AGM also approved a merit-based promotion-and-relegation system for umpires and confirmed Ranchi as the venue for the fifth Test against Australia in February 2027.

The Board of Control for Cricket in India pays about ₹3,000 crore in income tax every year, BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia disclosed on Friday at the board's 95th Annual General Meeting — a figure that drew applause from the state association representatives in the room. For a body that is frequently portrayed as a tax-free colossus, the number is a deliberate statement of scale.

A rebuttal to the tax-exemption narrative

Saikia's disclosure was aimed squarely at the perception that the world's richest cricket board pays little or no tax. The BCCI, unlike other sports federations in India, receives no government grants. The Central Information Commission has ruled that the board is not a public authority under the RTI Act, 2005, precisely because it takes no public funding. The ₹3,000-crore figure is consistent with the board's own books: financial statements circulated ahead of last year's AGM showed it had set aside ₹3,150 crore toward income-tax obligations for FY 2023-24, even while pursuing appeals in various tribunals.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=vqNdEgIyxqY

The Sports Act question

The timing is not accidental. The Supreme Court recently sought clarification from the BCCI on where it stands under the National Sports Governance Act, and Saikia made clear the board intends to cooperate once the government completes its part. "Regarding the Sports Act, our stand is very clear," he said, as quoted by Cricbuzz. "Once those exercises are completed and once the BCCI comes under the Sports Act, a particular notification has to be issued to make it a designated sport. Till that time, we are not supposed to do anything." He added that the board would file its clarification when the matter is listed next on October 27. Saikia also argued that because the BCCI pays taxes and takes no government funding, cricket cannot simply be treated as a 'designated sport' under the Act.

Umpires get a performance ladder

Beyond taxes, the AGM approved an enhanced payment structure for umpires and match referees, with officials reclassified into four grades — A, B, C and D — and a promotion-and-relegation system that will move 10 umpires up and 10 down at the end of every season based on assessed performance. Postings for knockout and high-profile matches will follow the same merit rankings.

"Ten umpires will go up, 10 umpires will go down. So, this will make them very alert throughout the season, and that will ultimately help the game of cricket, because some players' future depends on the decision of the umpire."

— Devajit Saikia, BCCI secretary

The AGM also settled the venue question for the fifth Test of the Border-Gavaskar Trophy against Australia: Ranchi will host it on February 19, 2027, with the five-Test series beginning in Nagpur on January 21, 2027, and travelling through Chennai, Guwahati and Ahmedabad. Separately, the board initiated planning for its centenary celebrations in 2028, with a year-long programme set to commence in December 2027.

Why it matters for the diaspora

For the millions of Indians abroad who fill stadiums and late-night streaming queues to watch the team, the ₹3,000-crore tax bill is a measure of the cricket economy that underwrites everything they consume — from IPL seasons to media rights that carry matches to living rooms in Edison and Fremont. The umpiring reforms, meanwhile, speak directly to the integrity of the contests diaspora fans argue about.

What's next

All eyes move to October 27, when the BCCI files its Supreme Court clarification on the Sports Act — a decision that will shape how the board is governed for years. Before that, the Border-Gavaskar Trophy in January will test both the team and the newly graded umpires under the new merit system.
